title: How this journal works
summary: The rules, the daily ritual, and the machinery behind a public learning journal — written down once so I can point at it.
text:
This site is a public record of learning to code, written one day at a time. This page explains the system behind it — partly for anyone curious, mostly so future-me cannot quietly renegotiate the rules.

The rules

One day, one entry. Between 150 and 300 words, in English, about what actually happened: what I studied, what confused me, what finally made sense. If the day went badly, the entry says so. The numbering counts entries, not calendar days — a missed day does not reset anything, it just means the next entry comes a day later. Guilt is not part of the system.

The title is the finding, never the number. "Day 12" tells you nothing. "What finally made list comprehensions click" tells you whether to read it. The day number lives in the metadata, where machine-facts belong.

Written here first. This site is the canonical archive. The same text goes out to LinkedIn as a post and to X as a thread, but those are copies for distribution. Platforms change their rules; this domain is mine.

The daily ritual

About fifteen minutes, most of it writing:
1. During the day: two or three lines of notes on my phone.

title: What finally made list comprehensions click
summary: I rewrote the same loop four times before I realised I had been reading it backwards.
text:
For a week I have been avoiding list comprehensions. Every time one appeared in someone else's code I mentally replaced it with a for loop and moved on. Today I stopped avoiding it.

What confused me was the order. In a normal loop I write the condition first and the result last. In a comprehension the result comes first, which felt like reading a sentence from the end.

squares = [n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]

Then I read it out loud in the order I would have written the loop: for every number in numbers, if it is even, give me its square. It was not backwards at all. Same sentence — the answer has simply been moved to the front, the way a newspaper headline puts the outcome before the explanation.

I rewrote four of my old loops as comprehensions. Two of them got clearer. The other two got worse: three conditions stacked into a single line that I could not read a minute later. I put those back.

That is the real lesson today. A comprehension is not a better loop. It is a shorter way to say a simple thing, and a bad way to say a complicated one. The choice is about the reader, not about looking clever.

title: I tried a security lab and understood nothing
summary: Six days into programming I opened a web security exercise. It was too early, and it was still worth it.
text:
Security is where I want to end up eventually, so today I opened a free web security lab to see what the destination looks like from here.

I understood almost none of it.

The exercise involved changing part of a web request to make a site behave differently. I could follow the individual words. I could not follow why any of it worked, because I do not yet know what a request is, what a parameter is, or what the site was supposed to do with either. It was like being handed a car engine before I had learned there was such a thing as a car.

I stopped after forty minutes, which I want to record as a decision rather than a failure. The gap was not "this is difficult". The gap was "I am missing the layer underneath".

Two things I am taking from it anyway.

The first is a corrected route. Before security comes the web: what a request is, what a response is, what a server does with the two. That is a prerequisite I did not know I was missing this morning.

The second is calibration. Nobody hires a beginner into security — the normal path is a few years as a developer first. Today made that concrete rather than theoretical. The destination is real, it is far, and the road to it goes thr

title: My first loop, and my first infinite one
summary: I wrote a while loop, forgot to change the thing it was checking, and learned what Ctrl-C is for.
text:
I wrote my first while loop today and immediately wrote my first infinite one.

count = 0
while count < 5:
    print("still going")

It printed forever. Thousands of lines, faster than I could read them, and my first genuine moment of panic at a computer in years — because I did not know how to make it stop. I closed the whole terminal window like someone unplugging a machine they are afraid of.

The missing line was obvious once I saw it: nothing ever changed count, so the condition stayed true forever. What was less obvious, and more useful, is the general shape of the mistake. A while loop has three parts that must agree — something that starts, something that gets checked, something that changes. I had written two of them and assumed the third.

Two things I now know that I did not this morning:

— Ctrl-C stops a running program. Closing the window is not required, and I am slightly embarrassed.
— A for loop over a range handles the changing part for you, which is presumably why everyone reaches for it first.

title: Swedish word order broke my confidence
summary: I can build the sentence correctly on paper and still get it wrong the moment I speak.
text:
Swedish is not optional for me. I need it for admission to Yrkeshögskola, which means it is graded, and a grade is not something enthusiasm can fix at the last minute. So it gets real hours, not leftover ones.

Today was word order, and specifically the rule that the verb wants to be in second position. On paper I can do this. Give me a sentence and thirty seconds and I will put igår first and the verb second and get it right.
Igår läste jag en bok.

Out loud, in a conversation, with someone waiting for me to finish — I put the verb wherever Russian or English would have put it. Every time. The knowledge is there and it does not arrive fast enough to be useful.

What I noticed today is that this is exactly the same problem as reading my own Python and seeing what I meant instead of what I wrote. In both cases I know the rule and my instinct overrides it before the rule gets a chance to speak.

The fix is presumably the same too: repetition until the correct version is the instinct, not the correction. Which is slow, and not very interesting to write about, and is going to be most of the next year in both subjects.

title: Reading documentation in English is its own skill
summary: I can read English news comfortably. Official docs turned out to be a different language entirely.
text:
I thought my English was good enough for this. Then I opened the official Python documentation.

It is not that the words are hard. It is that the sentences are built differently. News writing explains as it goes. Documentation assumes you already know the shape of what is being described and only tells you the parameters. A line like "returns a shallow copy of the list" contains three ideas I had to look up separately, and none of them were the difficult one.

The difficult one was "shallow". I know the word. I know it means not deep. I had no idea what it meant here, and no dictionary was going to tell me, because it is not really an English problem — it is a programming idea wearing an English word.

That is the useful distinction I found today. Some of what confuses me is vocabulary, and some of it is concepts hiding inside familiar vocabulary. When I mix them up I waste time in the wrong place, looking up words I already understand.

So I have started keeping two lists instead of one. Words I genuinely do not know go in the first. Words I know that are doing an unfamiliar job go in the second. The second list is much shorter and much more valuable.

title: Variables are boxes, and I opened the wrong one
summary: I spent an hour debugging a program that was doing exactly what I told it to do.
text:
Everyone says variables are the easy part. I wrote eleven lines today and none of them did what I expected.

The program was supposed to take a price, add tax, and print the total. It printed the price. Unchanged. Every time.

price = 100
total = price * 1.25
print(price)

I stared at this for a genuinely embarrassing amount of time. I checked my arithmetic. I checked that 1.25 was the right multiplier. I re-read the tax rate. The one thing I did not check was which box I was asking Python to open at the end.

It was doing exactly what I wrote. I had calculated total and then printed something else.

What I take from this is not "read your code more carefully" — I did read it, five times. It is that I was reading it as a description of my intention rather than as a list of instructions. In my head the last line meant "show me the answer". To Python it meant "show me price". Those are different sentences and only one of them is on the screen.

I am going to try saying each line out loud as an instruction from now on, not as a summary of what I meant.

Tomorrow, apparently, comes strings. I have been warned about quotation marks.

title: Installing Python took longer than my first program
summary: Two hours of paths and versions, then four seconds of actual programming.
text:
Today's plan was one line long: install Python. It took two hours.

Not because installing is hard, but because I did not understand what I was installing. I already had a Python on this machine, apparently, and the terminal kept answering a different version than the one I had just downloaded. I read about PATH four times before the sentence stopped being noise.

What finally helped was giving up on understanding it fully and just checking what the computer thought:

which python3
python3 --version

Two commands. They told me exactly which file was answering and which version it was. Everything I had been guessing at for an hour was printed in two lines.

Then I wrote the actual program:

print("Hello, Vassili")

Four seconds. It worked the first time. I sat there feeling slightly cheated, because the hard part had nothing to do with programming and everything to do with not knowing how to ask my own computer a question.

I think that is going to be the pattern for a while. The language will be the easy half. The environment around it — terminals, paths, versions, tools I have never heard of — is where the hours go.

title: Why I am starting this journal today
summary: I am 34, I have never written code, and I have decided to learn in public rather than quietly.
text:
I am 34. I have never written a line of code that did anything useful. Today I am starting, and I am doing it where people can see.

The quiet version of this plan failed twice already. Both times I bought a course, watched four hours of video, felt clever, and stopped within a month. Nothing existed afterwards to prove I had ever started, so quitting cost me nothing. That is the part I want to change.

So here is the rule I am giving myself. One entry every day. Between 150 and 300 words, in English, about what I actually did and what actually confused me. Not a tutorial, not advice — a record. If the day went badly, the entry says the day went badly.

Three things happen at once this way. I learn to program. I practise English, which I need because I am aiming at remote work rather than the local market. And I build something that exists whether or not I feel motivated on a given Tuesday.

I have done a long project before. It took two years and it was about my own body, not my head, but the shape was the same: something boring repeated for far longer than felt reasonable. I know what the middle of that feels like. I am counting on that memory more than on enthusiasm.
